title: Rhegmatogenous vs. Tractional Retinal Detachment: The Diagnostic Divide
summary: A high-yield comparative analysis of the two most common forms of retinal detachment. Distinguishing the mechanical pathophysiology is essential for surgical planning and visual prognosis.

sections.title: Clinical Features Comparison
content: RRD: Photopsias and floaters preceding shadow.
TRD: Gradual, progressive painless vision loss.
RRD: Shaffer sign (vitreous pigment) in 70% of acute cases.
TRD: History of PDR, Sickle Cell, or penetrating trauma.

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Presentation
content: Macula-ON status: Ophthalmic emergency requiring surgery <24 hours.
Acute drop in visual acuity (suggests macula-off).
Signs of PVD: Dense tobacco dust (Shaffer's) in anterior vitreous.
Intraocular Pressure: Paradoxical hypotony in chronic detachments.

sections.title: Investigation Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Dilated Indirect Ophthalmoscopy with scleral indentation.
Step 3: B-Scan Ultrasonography (mandatory if media is opaque).
Step 4: OCT Macula (confirming subretinal fluid vs. schisis).

content.explanation: B: Blind spot (visual field defect), R: Retinal tear, E: Elevation of retina, A: Acute onset, K: Kinetic mobility.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: In TRD, if there is a suspected break, it converts to a 'Combined RRD/TRD'—highly complex.
Scleral buckle is often favored in phakic patients for RRD to avoid cataract progression.
Membrane peeling in TRD must be done from posterior-to-anterior; delamination vs. segmentation.
Always check the fellow eye in RRD patients: 10-15% risk of bilateral involvement.
Peripheral retinoschisis is non-mobile and does not require surgery unless symptomatic and progressing toward macula.
